sentences.text: Mahajangasuchus was a medium to large crocodylomorph characterized by a broad snout, massive choanal septum, ziphodont teeth, and a short mandibular symphysis.
The dentary possessed 14 alveoli on each half, with the fourth and ninth being the largest.
The osteoderms featured deep irregular pits over their surface, except at the anterior margin where they overlapped the preceding osteoderm.
The osteoderms had strong keels and were subquadrangular to ovate, suggesting the dorsal armor consisted of no more than two rows.
Researchers provided different estimates for its size, with one suggesting it could measure up to 4 meters in length while another stated it weighed up to 360 kilograms.
The species epithet insignis is Latin for "remarkable" or "extraordinary," chosen to reflect the specimen's preservation and strange morphology.
Fossil evidence suggests subadult individuals were prey for the large snake Madtsoia madagascariensis, despite the risk of injury to the predator.
The genus Mahajangasuchus was described by Buckley and Brochu in 1998, following the discovery of the largest known specimen in 1995.
This well-preserved disarticulated skeleton was found about 1 km southeast of the village of Berivotra.
The species was formally named Mahajangasuchus insignis by Buckley and Brochu in 1999.
Research concluded that a large skeleton originally thought to be Trematochampsa oblita actually represented a new genus of crocodylomorph.
Mahajangasuchus likely lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle, which was a deviation from the typical terrestrial habits of its Notosuchian relatives.
Researchers suggest that the skull palate of Mahajangasuchus evolved to resist torsional forces while feeding.
The genus was initially placed in the family Trematochampsidae by Sereno et al. in 2001, but later reclassified into Peirosauridae by Turner and Calvo in 2005.
In 2009, Sereno and Larson classified Mahajangasuchus into its own family, Mahajangasuchidae, alongside the genus Kaprosuchus.
Later analyses returned Mahajangasuchus to a sister position with Kaprosuchus relative to peirosaurids, and the resulting clade takes a sister position to uruguaysuchids.
Mahajangasuchus lived during the Upper Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Mahajangasuchus have been found in the Maevarano Formation in northern Madagascar.
